messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
The quoted lines do not erase Majeed’s earlier character, but they do complicate it. He is still controlled, terse, and managerial: “Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village.” There is no apology, no softness, no emotional explanation. That brevity keeps his apathy partly visible. At the same time, he is physically carrying Jamila and deciding to move both women, which shows a protective responsibility rather than total indifference.

So yes, the same traits are present, but in a modified form. His cunning appears in the strategic, command-like tone: he makes the decision and expects Rahima to follow. His apathy appears in the lack of warmth; even the image of Jamila “wrapped in a thin quilt” is rendered more as practical burden than tender care. The “brilliant moonlight” that blinds him adds danger and urgency, but Majeed’s response remains efficient movement, not sentimental rescue.

On the deontology/teleology question, I would read the action as mainly teleological, with a small deontological undertone. A deontological interpretation would say he saves them because it is his duty, because protecting them is the right thing, or because he acts from good will regardless of consequences. A teleological interpretation says he acts because the outcome matters: reaching the village, avoiding immediate danger, preserving order, or preventing a worse result.

The text supports teleology more strongly because his speech is goal-directed: “I am going to take both of you to the village.” The focus is on destination and practical result, not moral principle. He does not state a rule, express guilt, or emphasize duty. Given his earlier cunning, it is plausible that he calculates that carrying them and leaving now is the safest course.

Still, it would be too simple to say he has no good will. If he were completely apathetic, he might ignore them or choose the easiest path for himself. By taking both of them, he acknowledges some responsibility. So the scene reads like pragmatic morality: he saves them not because his heart is suddenly soft, but because the calculated end—survival, order, or self-preservation—requires it. The good-will, if present, is quiet and instrumental.

radar
rotor
civic
refer
tenet
madam

reviver
